guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
The early practice is finding out who is actually in there: long reflection without external input, private journaling written without imagining a reader, time alone in nature, and the recovery of buried preferences—foods you really like, activities that feel good, beliefs you hold privately, and feelings that appear when nobody else is supplying the emotional cues.

Focusing can be especially useful for noticing feelings and preferences the conditioned self learned to overlook; you can then put tentative words to them, examine what they seem to mean, and revise your interpretation. Some people also benefit from temporary, intentional distance long enough for the conditioning to quiet down and authentic preferences to surface.

brief:
- the early practice is finding out who's actually in there: long reflection without outside input; private journaling written without imagining a reader; time alone in nature; and getting back buried preferences (foods you really like, things that feel good to do, beliefs you hold privately, and feelings that show up when nobody else is supplying the emotional cues)
- Focusing (Eugene Gendlin's method) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the conditioned self learned to overlook; you can then put tentative words to them, look at what they seem to mean, and revise how you read them
- some people also benefit from temporary, intentional distance, long enough for the conditioning to quiet down and real preferences to surface
